episodes.title: Why Excel TRIM Didn't Remove That Hidden Space #Shorts
source_linked_claims: TRIM only targets ASCII 32, not NBSP 160
scenes: You cleaned a name with Excel TRIM, but the hidden space remained. It might be a nonbreaking space.
Microsoft explains that TRIM handles normal ASCII spaces, but does not remove character one sixty by itself.
In this invented row, check the character code instead of repeatedly running the same formula.
Replace character one sixty with an ordinary space using SUBSTITUTE, then wrap the result in TRIM.
In the formula, substitute character one sixty with a normal space. Then wrap the result in TRIM, and compare it against your data.

episodes.title: Excel COUNT Says 2 but You Have 4 Values? Here's Why #Shorts
source_linked_claims: COUNT counts numeric values in a range while COUNTA counts nonempty cells
scenes: In this fictional Excel column, there are four filled cells, but COUNT returns only two. Why the mismatch?
Microsoft explains COUNT counts numeric entries in a range. Text labels are not counted as numbers.
COUNTA counts cells that contain data, including text. It answers a different question from COUNT.
Microsoft notes that COUNTA can count formulas returning empty text. Visually blank isn't always truly empty.
Use COUNT for numeric entries and COUNTA for nonempty entries. Check sample rows before trusting any total.

episodes.title: Excel Values Look the Same but Won't Match? Fix Hidden Characters
source_linked_claims: TRIM handles ASCII 32, not nonbreaking space 160; CLEAN and SUBSTITUTE can help
scenes: These two fictional names look identical. But a spreadsheet comparison can say they are different. The difference could be an invisible character, not a spelling error. Here is how to investigate without destroying the original data.

Text copied from websites or reports can contain characters that are hard to notice on a spreadsheet grid. Ordinary spaces and nonbreaking spaces are different character codes even when they appear visually similar.

Many people try TRIM and assume every space disappears. Microsoft explains that Excel's TRIM specifically handles the common ASCII space character thirty two. A nonbreaking space, character one sixty, may remain.

Measure text length before and after a cleanup formula. If two apparently identical values still have different lengths, check for hidden whitespace or control characters. The result is a clue, not proof of which character you have.

For ordinary extra spaces, TRIM can remove leading and trailing spaces and leave one between words. Keep a helper formula so you can see exactly what changed, instead of overwriting the imported field.

A nonbreaking space may survive TRIM. Microsoft documents using SUBSTITUTE to replace character one sixty with a regular space, then TRIM to normalize spacing. Confirm which code actually occurs in your file.
A practical formula replaces CHAR one sixty with a literal regular space using SUBSTITUTE, and wraps that result in TRIM. Copy the formula into a new column first and compare it with raw data.
The CLEAN function targets nonprinting characters. It is not a universal Unicode scrubber. If mismatches remain after CLEAN or TRIM, inspect the real characters before trying other formulas.

Another trap is converting text identifiers into numbers. An identifier that begins with zeros should generally remain text. Character cleanup and numeric type conversion are different operations with different risks.

Never overwrite the only copy of imported records before validating a cleanup. Use a helper column, keep the original, and compare a few exact values. You need to be able to explain every change later.

Use a simple, fictional before-and-after comparison. Once the correct hidden character has been replaced, the two intended keys can match. If they still differ, investigate case, formatting and source data.

The takeaway is to diagnose first: inspect visible text, compare lengths, identify the exact hidden character, and only then clean it. Keep a recoverable source and verify a sample before sharing your spreadsheet.
